en: He too will come out to escort you.
Of middle stature, broad in the shoulders,
If you look at him from the front,
He has the awe of six thousand warriors;
When he turns his back,
He has the form of a lion.
With a bright brow, bringing good fortune,
His stature towering like countless troops,
His face like buttered wheat,
His eyes like twilight mist,
Riding a horse like Akkula,
Wrapped in a pure white turban,
Your father Manas, the surpassing lion—
My foal, that is the place where he will support you.
If that sign appears,
Go on farther.
If that sign does not appear,
Go no farther; turn back.
Saying, 'I did not see the sign,'
Come and tell me, your unfortunate mother.
When you see that sign,
You may go farther on.
That is the place called Ken-Shor.
You will look upon Ken-Shor;
At the place where you turn,
This Ken-Shor of yours will come into view.
When you see that Ken-Shor,
Your heart will be sorely torn;
Tears will pour from your eyes.
That is the renowned place Ken-Shor.
I am the one who swallowed your father;
I was left behind at his head.
I devoured your father the khan
At the age of thirty-two.
Your father Manas was a lion;
A soul like your father, the one God
Would never create at all.
Of Mecca that girded its loins,
Your father was the backbone;
Of the still, vast realm of Islam,
Your father was the lion.
On his right, the Afghans,
It was your father who mowed them down;
On the uplands, the Chinese,
It was your father who slaughtered them.
He reached and struck the Afghans;
Untouched by your father's hand,
How could Zhet-Kait have remained unharmed?
Born in Altai, finding his people,
Your father Manas rose as khan;
Your father's voice struck souls from bodies.
Leading forty-two great hosts of troops,
Leading all those troops in abundance,
'Into gloomy Great Beijing
I shall go straight and thrust my spear,' he said.
'From a hell of grievous trouble,
I shall set souls free,' he said.
'I shall bring slaughter to Kakan,' he said.
'Esen Khan in Beijing—
I shall seize his khanship,' he said.
'I shall journey to Beijing,' he said.
'Esen Khan's daughter Burulcha,
That lovely, graceful one,
I shall seize from Beijing,' he said.
'On Beijing beyond the reach of the Flood,
I shall bring ceaseless slaughter,' he said.
'Of seething Beijing,
I shall seize the khanship,' he said.
The Muslim army went in great numbers;
Forty-two great hosts of troops went.
Into the gloomy land of Beijing
They went straight and thrust their spears;
Throughout Kakan's Beijing,
They fought six months without a pause.
Entering Kakan and turning back,
Your father, born a leopard,
Lost his many people.
Entering Beijing and turning back,
Losing his valiant people.
When he brought torment to Beijing,
When your father went to meet it,
Muzburchak and Khan Kokcho died;
Everyone who encountered Beijing died.
Ezhigei and Sheyren died together;
Kokotoy's giant named Bokmurun died.
The people who sent messengers died;
All who took part in the Beijing campaign died.
Many champions and giants died;
Mighty men no horse could bear died;
All who grappled with Beijing died together.
The road Khizir had traversed died;
Forty-two great hosts of troops died.
Entering Beijing and turning back,
When your father set out,
He lost his valiant warriors.
Entering Kakan and turning back,
Dark night fell upon your father.
Bereft of his leopard,
Your father, Sultan Khan Manas,
Lost Akkula to a bullet,
Let Almambet fall a martyr,
Had his wings broken,
And the one he relied upon,
Khan Chubak, he lost.
He ravaged Beijing and set his course;
As he faced the foe,
He devoured his valiant Khan Syrgak.
Leaving all his people strewn about,
When he conquered the people of Kakan,
Losing Akkula to a bullet,
Your noble, outstanding father,
When he was left helpless on foot,
His brother in faith in the other world,
His partner in what they gathered in this world,
My uncle, Prince Bakai,
Leading Arbuudan,
Bakai's many worries would not fit within his breast:
'He was a lion born a leopard;
Where shall I find his body?' he said.
Then his tears streamed in ten directions!
When he arrived, your leopard father was alive,
One of those who had not died.
Girding his waist securely,
Against seventy thousand Chinese,
Bakai arrived and attacked,
Making his presence plainly known.
There where he had reached your father,
He mounted him on Arbuudan.
Shouting, 'Manas, Manas!'
Raising 'Manas!' as his battle cry,
Breaking their defenses and attacking,
Khan Bakai then entered
And attacked the Chinese.
Their center, your mighty father
Cut through as he came;
Their two flanks, the warrior Bakai
Slaughtered his way along;
Their very center, your father the khan
Came and surrounded;
One side, Azhybai
Came and battered.
Shouting, 'Islam!'
Raising 'Islam!' as the battle cry,
Your dark, wolf-maned father,
Joining with Khan Bakai,
Pursued the Chinese,
Driving them toward Beijing.
At your father's hands died
The Chinese clad in iron-rope mail,
All their dagger-handed men.
Shypshaidar of the red whip,
Such a giant died at your father's hands,
The giant Tiken, son of Muzkindik,
A champion as huge as a mountain, died.
Apart from Konurbai,
All the mighty Chinese died together.
The Chinese fled in anguish,
Running toward Kakan;
Forty gates, great doors,
They barred securely.
While the Chinese stood hard pressed,
Your father forced his way in.
'With golden forelock and tasseled belt,
The only son of Khan Azozyl in Beijing,
The wolf-maned warrior Almambet—
How can I fail to avenge him?
This Konurbai of Alooke,
How can I fail to offer him as a sacrifice?
My companion, wolf-maned Chubak,
How can I fail to avenge him?
Esen Khan and Kary Khan in Beijing,
Both of them stretched at full length,
How, ah, can I fail to lay them low?'
Then the elder Bakai
Went and struck a door with his spear.
He brought down one door;
Azhybai went and struck once,
Went forth alone into battle.
Your leopard father struck once
And brought down seven doors.
Girding his waist tightly,
As he was about to break the door,
A voice sounded from the sky:
'Against Beijing beyond the Four Companions' reach,
Khan Manas, your strength is not enough; draw back!
To Beijing beyond Iskender's reach,
Your undertaking will not succeed; turn back.
To Beijing untouched by Sulayman,
Zulpukor cannot pierce; draw back.
The decree of the One God, Jappar,
Will be thus; behold it.
Your ribs will crack and split;
Your blood will be spilled in this place.
Better than that, Khan Manas,
Reach Talas and die there!'
When he led his troops and turned back,
Your leopard father, your protecting spirit,
When he turned back in mourning,
In Chatkal of vast Beijing,
In the marshes of the clear water,
Your father Manas the leopard,
When he dipped his hands into the water,
When he performed his ablution,
In the fortress of Beijing,
When the afternoon prayer time came,
When he turned his face northward,
When your father stood reciting his prayer,
Azhybai of the Argyn khan,
Six bowshots behind,
That guard, the Argyn khan's son,
Had let his eyes fall asleep.
With a cotton belt and broad boots,
The warrior Kalcha, khan of the monks,
Konurbai, mighty in cunning,
Had stalked your father and reached him.
Let me tell the rest:
Having spread his prayer mat,
Through the ridge of his back,
Your father, Khan Manas,
Was stabbed, his lung pierced through.
Azhybai of the Argyn khan,
Unable to hold still for fright,
Turned Kartkuron's head
And thrust his spear at Kalcha.
A blue-mottled star in the sky was eclipsed;
Konurbai, whose horse was swift,
Fled in plain sight and escaped.
The spear was left in the back;
Flustered and hurrying, Akybai
Twisted and pulled the spear out.
The steel point cracked
And broke off in the backbone.
My warrior did not speak of his wound
And thus brought this wretched woman misery.
Had I been a man instead of a woman,
My darling orphan,
Had I been your father's watchman,
Had I been the warrior Azhybai,
Would I not have marked out my resolve!
With his cotton belt and broad boots,
That swine, the monks' khan,
Would I not have shown him some sport!
Would I not have tested the swift horse,
Stabbing that rotten wretch from behind,
Would I not have made Beijing endure
A spectacle of slaughter and upheaval!
The spearhead was barbed;
Your father kept it unspoken,
Digging my pit deep,
Boiling misery for me.
Let him rot and die
The spear point left within him
Had shown your father a terrible spectacle.
Your father coughed in sharp bursts,
Lifting his head from the pillow.
When he raised his head and cried 'Ah!'
